hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to **prominent, high-contrast dark linear features**—specifically **horizontal or diagonal bands, stripes, grooves, or elongated gaps**—traversing a lighter surface. The activating features are consistently **deep black, dark charcoal, or dark gray**, creating a sharp luminosity contrast against backgrounds or adjacent areas of **white, light gray, silver, or pale metallic tones**. This selectivity encompasses a wide range of semantic concepts, including painted stripes on vehicles, atmospheric bands on planets, structural recesses in machinery, and biological markings like a lateral line on a fish, provided the visual pattern of a dark line intersecting a lighter field is present. The neuron remains invariant to object identity, surface texture, and slight curvature, focusing instead on the geometry of the stratification or separation. The activating feature typically spans **60–100% of the image width** (or diagonal length) while occupying a narrower vertical segment of approximately **5–20% of the image height**, often positioned centrally or arranged in parallel stacks.
